source.title: From Knots to Knobs: Towards Steerable Collaborative Filtering Using Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Martin Spišák; Ladislav Peška; Petr Skoda; Vojtěch Vančura; Rodrigo Alves

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table content is flattened, so individual tag-level assignments in Table 2 cannot all be reliably attributed.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE neurons in collaborative-filtering models correspond selectively to semantic concepts, using tag–activation statistics rather than the toy-network geometric measurements in the original superposition work. It does not test superposition geometry or capacity competition.
record.gate_note: Only V5 is tested, and only the semantic-correspondence aspect: the study measures how selectively SAE neurons map to item tags. It does not test feature completeness, stability across training runs or data, or whether SAE features are canonical units. The reconstruction and recommendation-steering results are not rows for the listed claim versions. No results test feature-over-dimension capacity, near-orthogonal directions, or LLM activations.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool to make collaborative-filtering autoencoder (CFAE) recommenders steerable. It reports reconstruction fidelity, tag–neuron selectivity and steering performance for its pipeline. None of its results bear on a version as stated. No toy-model geometry or capacity tests (V1, V2). No alternative causes of polysemanticity (V3). The systems are recommender CFAEs, not LLMs (V4). Tag selectivity of SAE neurons does not measure whether dictionary features are complete, stable or canonical units (V5). No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features (V6). The interpretability results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SAE sparse layers in CFAEs are "largely monosemantic" and that metadata-based mappings yield interpretable concept–neuron links usable for steering. TopK SAEs preserve nearly all accuracy for cosine-like (ELSA) embeddings, while MultVAE is less robust to sparse reconstruction and steering. They add that not all CF architectures suit SAE hooks.
record.recipe_differences: The study inserts and evaluates SAEs within collaborative-filtering autoencoders; it does not use the toy-network feature-generation or geometric analysis recipe from the original superposition work.
record.method_sensitivity: Semantic selectivity and steering differ across CFAE architecture, SAE reconstruction loss, and tag–neuron mapping strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: TopK SAEs (8192 latents, k=16) trained on 1024-d CFAE user embeddings (ELSA, MultVAE) on ML-25M yield neurons with selective tag activations. Many tags fall below the per-model average entropy. The share of tags with D_KL > 10 is 88%, 59% and 88% across the three configurations. Selectivity varies with backbone and reconstruction loss, and MultVAE argmax mappings overlap heavily across tags.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs recover sparse, semantically selective features from non-language (collaborative-filtering) embeddings, with selectivity dependent on architecture and SAE loss.

record.problems: The semantic analysis uses one dataset's item tags and three selected SAE configurations. The paper notes mapping overlaps and coarse or ambiguous concepts; it does not assess feature completeness or stability across runs. The paper reports uncertainty for some recommendation metrics, but not for the tag–neuron selectivity results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 gives per-tag high/low examples, but its flattened presentation does not permit reliable assignment of all entries to model configurations. Reconstruction and steering outcomes were left out because they do not measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All: toy models, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition, importance-dependent dedicated vs shared dimensions.
All: no LLM activations studied; SAE recovery is shown only in recommender CFAE embeddings.
Completeness, stability across seeds or data, and canonicality of SAE features are not measured. Only tag selectivity is measured.
All: no 1-D vs multi-dimensional feature analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V5 and labelled limits_scope. That conflates semantic interpretability of SAE neurons with V5's claim that SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units, which the study never measures. V4 is restricted to LLMs, and this study uses recommender models. The results are better treated as a cross-domain interpretability finding. Reconstruction and steering results were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The models studied are recommender-system CFAEs, not LLMs; LLM feature spread and SAE recovery in LLMs are not tested.
Semantic tag–neuron correspondence is measured, but feature completeness, stability across runs or settings, and canonicality as the model's full representation units are not tested.
The study does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: MultVAE+L2
rows.stage_stated: Trained CFAE; SAE trained on its user embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Measured entropy of tag-to-neuron activation distributions

conditions.value: TopK, k=16, 8× width, L2 reconstruction loss

rows.value: H = 6.3; a large portion of tags had lower entropy than this average
rows.note: The authors interpret lower-entropy tag distributions as more selective activation patterns; the fraction described as a large portion is not quantified here.
rows.check: Tag-entropy selectivity of SAE neurons in a recommender CFAE. Wrong system for V4 (not an LLM), and the measure does not address V5's completeness, stability or canonicality. H = 6.3 is the per-model average used as reference, not a result against a baseline.

rows.subject: ELSA+L2
rows.stage_stated: Trained CFAE; SAE trained on its user embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Counted unique tags and neurons selected as each other's most distinctive match
rows.value: 834 unique neurons were most specific for at least one tag; 985 unique tags were most distinctive for at least one neuron
rows.note: The paper also notes overlaps among matches, including cases where one neuron is selected for multiple related tags.
rows.check: Count of distinctive argmax matches (834 neurons, 985 tags) in ELSA+L2. No denominator is given for active neurons or tags, and it bears on no listed version. The mapping uses argmax_t M_n→t and argmax_n M_t→n.

rows.subject: ELSA+L2
rows.stage_stated: Trained CFAE; SAE trained on its user embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Examined overlap among the most distinctive tag–neuron mappings
rows.measure: Number and nature of tags sharing a top-neuron mapping
rows.value: Neuron id3125 was the top neuron for “space action”, “space adventure”, and “classic sci-fi”
rows.note: The authors discuss this overlap as a limitation in granularity, potentially related to ambiguous concepts, data, or SAE expressiveness.
rows.check: A single qualitative example (neuron id3125 serving three space tags). Illustrative only. The authors attribute it mainly to tag ambiguity and popularity bias, not to feature granularity of the model.
